[[RunningHead]]

Clinical Observations: Treatment Issues in the Impulse Disorders

Problems which surround the handling of impulsive behavior are of major concern in contemporary American society. Modern Psychoanalysis presents three papers dealing with related issues as they appear in the psychoanalytic treatment situation.

Robert Unger reviews some approaches to the treatment of alcoholism. He reports that the addictive process is amenable to psychological influence if the analyst employs special techniques to induce a transference, and if he deals with the difficult counter-transference feelings that result.

Eugene Goldwater considers the special challenges in working with acting out patients rather than the inhibited patients of classical psychoanalysis. He presents a general theoretical model for treatment of impulse disorders, such as drug addiction and alcoholism. Case examples illustrate the use of this model.

Arnold Bernstein deals with the obverse side of this problem, which is the analyst's fear of acting impulsively and how this may become an obstacle to resolving a resistance.

Philosophy of Education in Institute Training

Isabelle Hanigsberg

Isabelle Hanigsberg

42 North Drive
Great Neck, New York, 11021

Isabelle Hanigsberg  

The founding of the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies was conceived as another step in the attempt to find a solution to the problem of analytic training. Balint (1965), in discussing analytic training says:

The greatest mistake we could make would be to consider our present training system as a final solution to our many problems. In fact, this is far from being the truth. The present system is only one more step in a long development after many previous steps have been found faulty in one respect or another, and it is quite certain that future generations will form the same opinions of our present system (p. 275).

To provide material for a history of the formation of the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies, with its particular philosophy of education, training and treatment, its founders were asked to respond to a number of questions. Some of the questions and responses follow.

Why did you feel the need to establish a new psychoanalytic training institute?

Most of the founders agreed that they were interested in establishing an institute where students could be trained to deal with the narcissistic disorders they were increasingly seeing in treatment (in addition to the oedipal disorders).

Research: The Training of Psychoanalysts

This is another installment of an ongoing section devoted to the subject of research. The following five articles represent thinking on the current status of research in psychoanalytic education and training. An ongoing question in psychoanalysis concerns who is qualified to practice and how the training should be conducted. The articles by psychoanalysts which follow are concerned with these issues.

Yonata Feldman recounts her participation in one of the earlier efforts to train social workers to work with resistance and to undertake a therapeutic rather than a supportive role with their clients, whose diagnosis was mainly borderline. Deborah P. Margolis traces the European and American history of approaches to the training of psychoanalysts, and the controversy around the question of lay analysis.

Further ideas on training are selected from a conference on that subject sponsored by the National Accreditation Association for Psychoanalysis. Members of Jungian, Reikian, Adlerian and Modern Psychoanalytic institutes participated, and the diverse views of Jonathan Goldberg, Alan Roland, Robert Ellenbogen and Hyman Spotnitz are presented here.

E. D.

E. D.

E. D.  

Medard Boss presents a phenomenological approach to dream interpretation. He proposes a revision of the classical Freudian assumption that a distinction must be made between manifest and latent dream content. Instead, he holds that the dream be viewed from the dreamer's perception as it actually presents itself in the dream. This allows for an evaluation of the extent to which the dreamer's “field of vision” remains open or closed, as well as an examination of the dreamer's relationship to what he is encountering. Consequently, it makes possible a definition of the dreamer's existential structure, with its limitations and barriers.

Experiments are presented in which dreams are induced by hypnotic suggestion in both normal and neurotic subjects. The results indicate that symbolism and disguise operate to a greater degree in neurotic subjects: The dreams of normal subjects present more direct expression of the dream wish.

The book enables the reader to gain a clear understanding of the phenomenological approach by providing 36 concrete “dream examples” of healthy, neurotic, braindamaged, melancholic and schizophrenic patients.

Harold Davis

Harold Davis

Harold Davis  

The authors have looked back over twenty years of working together as conjoint therapists and have produced a really excellent exposition of this mode of psychoanalytic therapy in which the patient is treated concurrently in individual and group analysis by two different therapists who compare notes on a regular basis. Conjoint therapy is a refinement of the more usual “combined therapy” in which the patient is treated individually and in group by the same therapist. The authors would heartily agree with the notion that combined therapy offers the patient the best of both types of experience, individual and group. In combined therapy the group provides the patient with a laboratory in which he is usually quickly confronted with his problems in relationships, motivating him to work on them in depth in his individual hour. Improvements in his ego functioning can then be taken back to the group and tested out. The authors' argument is that it is even better if the individual analyst and the group analyst are not the same person but two different therapists who work in close consultation. One advantage claimed is that having two therapists helps the patient experience the dynamics of the parental triangle.

E. D.

E. D.

E. D.  

This is an illuminating and entertaining book on the sociology of psychoanalysis in France over the past decade. Freud wrote that the “final and decisive battle” for psychoanalysis would be waged “where the greatest resistance has been displayed.” France, with greater tenacity than any other western country, has resisted the integration of psychoanalysis into its intellectual and cultural life for more than half a century. Turkle's book provides a thorough analysis of the belated resolution of that resistance and of the resultant “progressive communication,” which has since taken place between French culture and psycoanalytic theory. Turkle dates the beginning of Freud's “French revolution” with the student upheavals of 1968. Since then under the leadership of the “French Freud,” Jacques Lacan, psychoanalysis has invaded every aspect of French culture, thought and politics and in turn has itself been recast in the characteristic French image—a dramatic fusion of science and poetry. A major achievement of this book is the lucid exposition which Turkle provides of Jacques Lacan's linguistically based psychoanalytic theory.

The writings of Carl Jung have had much to say about his theory of dreams and dream interpretation. He considered dreams to be of central importance in understanding his patients and in the analytic process. However, unlike Freud, he never addressed himself directly to a theory of dreams and brought his thoughts on the subject together under one roof. His theory of dreams has been scattered through 20 volumes of his writings, in 972 separate entries.

Mary Ann Mattoon has remedied this situation. Through a thorough search of Jung's published and unpublished writings, Mattoon has compounded a systematic and comprehensive presentation of Jung's theory of dream interpretation.

The author of this book is a Dutch psychiatrist who has written a readable, often fascinating and sometimes shocking book on medical ethics. While van den Berg is concerned almost exclusively with issues such as medication and surgery pertinent to a medical practice, he makes a strong

appeal for physicians to include emotional understanding of their patients when they make ethical judgments. He illustrates this appeal with a number of examples describing the usual way, contrasted with what he thinks is a preferable way of telling a patient that she has cancer or that some radical surgical procedure might be needed to prolong her life. News and Notes

June Bernstein and Jane Goldberg

Jane Goldberg

Jane Goldberg  

Several recent conferences around the New York City area have explored issues relevant to modern psychoanalysis. The use and misuse of countertransference was the subject of a conference sponsored by the Advanced Institute for Analytic Psychotherapy. Panelists who offered their views included Peter Giovacchini, Susan Issacs Elmhirst, Harold Searles, W.W. Meisner, and Vamik Volkan.

Several of the comments addressed the issue of the meaning of “transfer” of feelings—from patient to analyst or analyst to patient. The possibility of this mechanism being literal was suggested in a case history presentation by Giovacchini. He related the story of a patient who suffered from hay fever so severe that he found it necessary to leave the city every summer. After three years of analysis, Giovacchini realized the patient had not taken his habitual annual leave at any point in the analysis. Curious, he asked the patient why. The patient did not know why his hay fever disappeared, but thereafter Giovacchini found himself suffering from a dust allergy. It would seem, then, that the analyst's literal assumption of the patient's symptomology had occurred.

Searles, too, referred to the analyst's need to experience the feelings of the patient. In commenting on symbiotic strivings in the patient, he suggested that in order for individuation to occur, the analyst must come to experience these symbiotic feelings as belonging more to himself than to the patient.

This compilation is well described by its title and subtitle. It comes highly recommended by Vamik Volkan and Sydney E. Pulver in dust-jacket blurbs and by Nathaniel Ross in a foreword. Socarides has assembled 31 papers dealing with specific affective states, none of them new and many familiar, all by classical Freudians, including Zilboorg, Deutsch, Greenson, Bergler, Bion, Kris. These are clinical studies: affects as reported and manifested in the analytic situation by the patient, are considered. Predictably in a classically oriented book, countertransference affects are nowhere considered. Lucid commentaries by Socarides accompany every contribution. Papers are arranged chronologically, from a historically important contribution on depression by Sandor Rado (1927) to one by James Alexander on horror (1972). This arrangement is possibly as good as any, but does not appear to be purposeful—that is, Socarides does not attempt to adduce an evolution of psychoanalytic understanding of affects. The selection is generous, amounting to about 220,000 words and is presented with ample type size and margins.

This book provides a wide range of data about dissociated states such as fugue, multiple personality, amnesia, dreaming, hallucination, automatic writing and age regression. Hilgard examines these states as they present themselves in everyday life and as produced in the laboratory with the aid of hypnotic procedures. Based on his laboratory findings he proposes a reexamination of the classical theory of dissociation.

In experiments using hypnosis for pain reduction, Hilgard shows that two channels of information can be processed parallelly. The hypnotized person may feel no pain, but a concealed part of him registers and stores information about it which is then revealed by special techniques like automatic writing and automatic talking. Hilgard produces evidence to support his premise that this “hidden observer” represents a form of consciousness quite different from the conscious-unconscious model presented by Freud and Jung.

Yonata Feldman  

The aim of this presentation is to describe the experiences of a group of social workers at the Jewish Board of Guardians while training to learn to understand and treat borderline psychotic children and their parents. This project was conducted under the leadership of Dr. Hyman Spotnitz as consulting and training psychiatrist at the Bronx office of the Madeline Borg Child Guidance Institute during the years 1944-1954.

When the idea emerged that delinquent children whose behavior in various correctional settings for Jewish children had improved, and who were ready for discharge, needed help in readjusting to family, friends, and the community, a city office was opened for that purpose. First called the Office of Field Activities, it was later named the Jewish Board of Guardians. With the development of new ideas in child psychiatry and especially in child guidance, and the emergence of new hypotheses about human behavior and its disorders, the agency turned its attention to prevention.

In 1926 the JBG sponsored demonstration projects in two schools, whose purpose was to detect behavioral problems in children before problems could emerge. That same year a special Child Guidance Department was organized to apply a psychiatric approach to the study of children. Most psychoanalytic formulations about motivation for treatment are conceptually loose and beset with internal contradictions. That library of dusty ideas usually beclouds efforts to understand what actually transpires in the consulting room. Even a crude classification system can improve the state of affairs, if it makes operational distinctions between various procedures intended to facilitate the patient's motivation to learn and to change.

Clinical explicitness affords opportunity to test and select which strategy best meets the demands of the concrete therapeutic task.

As a modest beginning, I suggest a tripartite division which applies to most treatment approaches. First, there are motivational schema which are what academic psychologists would call negative or aversive reinforcement theories or, in a lighter vein, “stick” theories. Then there are positive reinforcement or reward approaches (the “carrot” principle). Finally come those relatively newer conceptualizations of the learning process in terms of intrinsic motivation or optimal excitation, which I am tempted to label “umbrella” theories. Having proposed a classification system, however, it becomes necessary to translate it into clinical terms.

Negative motivation (stick) theories such as the classic position of Freud, rest on the premise that the most effective spur to learning is the internal cudgel of the patient's own discomfort.

In January of 1907, Max Eitingon, a medical student in Zurich, came to Vienna with one of his more seriously disturbed patients to consult with Dr. Sigmund Freud. Like other physicians who had become familiar, chiefly through his writings, with the creator of the new psychology, Eitingon was eager for enlightenment and guidance from the living source. Although the patient was pronounced unsuitable for analytic treatment, Eitingon's visit to Vienna was not without its rewards. In those halcyon days of psychoanalysis when that far country with which it dealt was yet trackless save for the inroads made into it by its discoverer, the handful of adherents who had gathered around Freud met with him every Wednesday evening in his waiting room. And here Eitingon was invited to join them, the pioneering few, as they sat around the rectangular table, to talk, argue, discuss, present cases, project plans, ideas, areas for research, like all pioneers in movements extending the frontiers into the unexplored. Eitingon remained in Vienna for about a fortnight, not only attending the Wednesday evening meetings, but enjoying yet another privilege. “He passed three or four evenings with Freud,” says Jones, “and they were spent in personal analytic work during their long walks in the city. Such was the first training analysis!” (Jones, 1955) It should be added that Eitingon's training analysis did not end in the winter of 1907.

Winnicott had written this intimate account of his psychoanalytic treatment of a young girl some ten years ago and it is now republished. It is a clinical and verbatim description of the analysis of a young girl, which is begun when she was two years and three months old. She was seen for sixteen sessions, utilizing the “on demand” method, until she was five years old. The presenting problem was fantasies that kept her awake at night. The “on demand” method was a departure for Winnicott since he was an orthodox analyst, though with Kleinian leanings. In spite of the non-traditional schedule of visits, he defines this case as an analysis because he “directed attention to the transference and the unconscious, not to the formal arrangements of the analytic situation, or the frequency or regularity of the analytic sessions.”

Progressive movement was evidenced in the ongoing process of each session. On each occasion this child brought a problem she was able to manifest and to work on, and Dr. Winnicott observed her play and interpreted the unconscious material that was causing her discomfort and hindering her development.

Her parents' letters are included and they provide a description of her behavior at home. The evolution of the meaning and use of the couch in analytic treatment is examined by the author, a practicing psychoanalyst and founder of the Philadelphia School of Psychoanalysis. Stern creatively pursues theoretical and clinical aspects of the use of the couch in order to gain an understanding of “how the process of symbolization has seized upon the couch both to obfuscate and highlight its true significance” (p. 13).

Stern reviews the cultural implications of the use of the couch from the perspectives of various psychotherapeutic modalities and patients. In our culture, the patient who “lies down” is symbolic of a passive attitude toward authority. Stern suggests that by choosing the couch as a clinical tool, Freud invited a passivity associated with the feminine personality, while at the same time providing access to the patient's mind undistracted by visual stimuli. Passivity and protection from stimuli may be seen as recreating the physical conditions for the rebirth of the mind.

In discussing the significance of jokes about the couch, Stern points out the relationship of humor to the direct expression of aggression and sexuality. The unconscious expectations of the passive, reclining patient are disappointed by the inactivity of the analyst who merely listens when the patient expects he will actively “do something” to effect a cure.

History

Countertransference is a phenomenon whose existence was recognized very early in the history of psychoanalysis. Freud (1910, 1915) gave the term to the unconscious reactions of the analyst to his patient, resulting from the analyst's own unresolved unconscious conflicts. He considered it an unwelcome intrusion which interfered with the objective conduct of the analysis, and he recommended that the analyst make efforts to overcome it. With some exceptions, this view prevailed in analytic circles until fairly recently. Beginning in the 1950's, however, modifications of this attitude began to appear as some early investigators (A. Reich, 1951; Gitelson, 1952) noted the importance of countertransference in the analytic process. This trend became more pronounced with the development of ego psychology and object relations theory and their applications in the treatment of schizophrenia and the borderline disorders in general (Fromm-Reichman, 1952; Rosenfeld, 1952; Searles, 1967). At the present time, it is safe to say that countertransference has come to be recognized as a significant component in the therapy of narcissistic disorders.

Kernberg (1975), reviewing the literature, finds two contrasting approaches to the concept, the classical and the totalistic. The former adheres essentially to Freud's views.

Arnold Bernstein  

Psychoanalysts take it for granted that once therapy has begun, clients should be prohibited or at least discouraged from “acting out” either within or between their sessions. Instead of taking action on the basis of any of their impulses, thoughts or feelings, clients are instructed to postpone them and put them into words. There are, of course, a number of sound theoretical as well as practical reasons for doing this, but these are so widely known that nothing would be served by repeating them here. Nevertheless, therapists who enforce this proscription too literally are likely to be acting out their own neurotic anxieties and countertransference resistances.

“One best protects the patient from disasters brought about by carrying his impulses into action,” Freud (1914) says, “by making him promise to form no important decisions affecting his life during the course of treatment, for instance, choice of a profession or of a permanent love-object, but to postpone all such projects until after recovery.” But Freud's motives for offering this advice are partially practical rather than purely analytic, since his avowed purpose is to protect patients from themselves, “until after recovery.”

In the 1920's, Ella Freeman Sharpe, having spent most of her fifty-plus years as a student and teacher of literature, went to Vienna to become a student of psychoanalysis. In 1937 the Hogarth Press published Dream Analysis, a collection of lectures Sharpe gave at the London Institute of Psychoanalysis. In 1950 Hogarth published Collected Papers on Psycho-Analysis. Both volumes have been out of print for some years and it is to Brunner-Mazel's credit that they are being republished at the present time, because their value to present day psychoanalysis is inestimable. The ability to make contact is a critical element in the processes of separation-individuation and libido-object constancy formation (Fraiberg, 1969; A. Freud, 1968; Mahler, 1968, 1972a, 1972b, 1975; Spitz, 1965). The ways in which a young child contacts or avoids contacting the primary object, usually the mother, are significant (Bowlby 1969, 1973).

Modern psychoanalytic theory offers a major technical innovation called contact functioning:

To permit the narcissistic transference to develop fully, interventions are cued to the patient's verbal attempts to solicit some information about his characteristic preoccupations, to satisfy his personal interest in the practitioner, or to convert silence or monologue into dialogue through a casual question. W. Goldwater

W. Goldwater

9 Forest Edge Road

W. Goldwater  

The Problem of the Impulsive Patient

Psychoanalysis originated in the verbal study and treatment of persons suffering from a pathological excess of inhibitions. The classical psychoanalytic technique which was developed for these overcontrolled patients involved subjecting them to moderate levels of anxiety and frustration: anxiety induced by free association and by ego-oriented questions and interpretations, frustration caused by the neutrality of the analyst and by the strict limitations on the types of interactions that were permissible between patient and analyst. Patients whose egos are relatively strong, whose capacity for object transference is well developed, and in whom aggressive drives present relatively less of a threat than libidinal ones, can benefit from classical psychoanalysis.

Modern psychoanalytic theory and technique originally was formulated to deal with schizophrenic patients (Spotnitz, 1969). These patients are for the most part overcontrolled, but are subject to periods of ego breakdown resulting in a psychotic state. They cannot tolerate the anxiety induced by the ego-oriented classical technique.

In the spring of 1971, modern psychoanalytic theory was introduced to the community in a series of sixteen lectures. This was the first step in the development of organized modern psychoanalytic teaching. Before the lectures, psychoanalysts trained in modern techniques had taught at psychoanalytic institutes and had conducted workshops, courses, and conferences in universities and social agencies, but resistances in administration, in fellow-faculty members, as well as in students were difficult to resolve.

The lecture series was followed by the founding of the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies. Seven years have passed since this experiment in modern psychoanalytic education began. So far as we know, no other institute is studying how psychoanalytic skills are acquired in the classroom or how best to convey scientific precepts, integrate principles with concepts and translate theory into emotional discovery.

As faculty worked together to train candidates for teaching, research and psychoanalytic practice, blocks in learning about emotional conflicts, defenses and behavior were discovered. It became clear that teaching methods would have to confront these resistances to learning before content could be effectively conveyed.

An interesting class mixture resulted from the institute's policy of open admission to what was then called the preanalytic program.

Linda Gochfeld

Linda Gochfeld

P.O. Box 440
Kingston, N.J., 08528

Linda Gochfeld  

Historically there have been two distinct streams in thought and investigation about emotional disorders: the physiological and the psychological. Freud, who began as a neurologist, was well acquainted with both, and even suggested that his psychological approach might give way to later physiological knowledge:

Here we are concerned with therapy only in so far as it works by psychological means, and for the time being we have no other. The future may teach us to exercise a direct influence, by means of particular chemical substances, on the amounts of energy and their distribution in the neural apparatus. (1938, p. 182)

Investigations in the two fields are conducted with different methods and usually by different people. As in the proverbial case of the blind men and the elephant, a person with an emotional disorder may receive quite different diagnoses and treatments depending on the orientation of the treating therapist.

In recent years, the most productive physiological line of endeavor has been in the field of psychopharmacology, the treatment of emotional disorders with drugs. These drugs have in part fulfilled Freud's prediction: they do alter levels of energy by influencing neurotransmitters in the brain. Through such treatment, hundreds of thousands of patients have been released from state mental hospitals and have been enabled to lead productive lives.

Sustaining Transference in the Treatment of Alcoholism

Robert Unger

Robert Unger

222 Park Avenue South
New York, N.Y. 10003

Robert Unger  

Psychoanalysis is not usually considered to be an effective tool in dealing with alcoholism. It is a therapy mode that is rarely sought by the alcoholic, and is looked on with disfavor by the alcoholism treatment community. The image is often of the cold, intellecutual and emotionless analyst, who is primarily interested in the past. Some of these preconceptions are true: the analyst is there to analyze rather than to gratify. People with impulse disorders, such as alcoholism, are likely to attribute coldness and lack of concern to anyone who is not gratifying.

Most treatment of alcoholics deals with trying to improve the alcoholic's life, and solving the problems created by the drinking. While this process may be gratifying enough to the patient to keep him in treatment for a while, the underlying impulse disorder is not addressed. I have found in my work that the alcohlic does need gratification from the analyst. If the analytic situation is experienced as too frustrating, the patient will either leave treatment prematurely, interminably continue the drinking pattern, or discover some new way of destructively acting out his impulses. Traditional analytic approaches need to be modified, then, so that sufficient gratification can be provided to prevent a more serious regression or termination of the treatment.

Bacterial Invasions and the Narcissistic Transference

Jeremy Bernstein's profile on Dr. Lewis Thomas, Biology Watcher (New Yorker: Jan. 2, 1978), provides some unexpected connections between biomedical research and current psychoanalytic theory. Readers of Thomas' book, Lives of a Cell, may recall his assertion that it takes prolonged intimacy before one kind of creature can cause illness in another. He now proposes that infectious disease is caused by a misreading of signals between invader and host. Familiarity comes first: “For signals to be misread they must first be read. If a signal is too strange, it will simply be ignored.” Dr. Thomas felt that the precautions taken against infection from the moon were unnecessary. His views suggest something like a narcissistic transference as the basis for any kind of influence from the outside. In terms that sound familiar to a psychoanalyst, Thomas says: “Disease usually results from inconclusive negotiations for symbiosis … a biological misinterpretation of borders.” Furthermore, it appears that the “defense reactions of the cells” release the very poisons that are most dangerous to their survival. Thomas describes the mobilization of such defenses as being “something like a panic.” He says there are few diseases in which the invading bacteria do as much cell damage as overreaction on the part of the host.
